topic: Softmax and Categorical Cross-Entropy Loss: Full Derivation of the Gradient dL/dz = (softmax − one-hot)
overview:
In a segmentation network like the U-Net used for BraTS post-treatment glioma segmentation, the final layer produces, for every voxel, a vector of raw real-valued scores called **logits** — one score per class (e.g., background, enhancing tumor, non-enhancing tumor core, edema, resection cavity). These scores are unbounded and do not form a probability distribution. Two operations turn them into a usable training signal: **softmax**, which squashes the logits into positive numbers that sum to 1 (a probability distribution over classes), and **categorical cross-entropy**, which measures how far that predicted distribution is from the known correct label. Ronneberger et al.'s original U-Net paper (MICCAI 2015) defines exactly this: a pixel-wise softmax over the final feature map combined with a cross-entropy loss as the network's "energy function."

The centerpiece of this note is a small mathematical miracle that makes deep learning practical: when you compose softmax with cross-entropy and differentiate the loss with respect to the raw logits z, all the messy intermediate terms cancel and you are left with the strikingly simple expression **dL/dz = p − y**, where p is the softmax output (the predicted probabilities) and y is the one-hot encoded ground-truth label. In words: the gradient pushed back into the network is simply "predicted probability minus target," clipped between −1 and +1 per class. This is why the softmax+cross-entropy pair is numerically well-behaved and is implemented as a single fused operation in every framework (PyTorch's `CrossEntropyLoss`, TensorFlow's `softmax_cross_entropy_with_logits`).

This document derives that result with no algebra skipped: first the softmax Jacobian ∂pᵢ/∂zⱼ = pᵢ(δᵢⱼ − pⱼ), then the cross-entropy derivative ∂L/∂pᵢ = −yᵢ/pᵢ, then the chain-rule composition that collapses to p − y using the single fact that the one-hot label sums to one. Worked numeric examples with small concrete vectors make every substitution explicit, and the gotchas cover numerical stability (the log-sum-exp trick), the log(0) hazard, and why binary and multi-class forms coincide.

key_points.point: Softmax converts a vector of K real-valued logits into a probability distribution: each output is positive and the K outputs sum to exactly 1. It is the multi-class generalization of the logistic sigmoid.
key_points.source: Goodfellow, Bengio, Courville, Deep Learning (2016), Ch. 6.2.2

key_points.point: Categorical cross-entropy for a single example is L = -Σ_i y_i log(p_i); with a one-hot label it reduces to L = -log(p_c), the negative log-probability the model assigned to the true class c. This is exactly the negative log-likelihood of the correct label.
key_points.source: Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning (2006), Ch. 4.3.4

key_points.point: The softmax Jacobian is ∂p_i/∂z_j = p_i(δ_ij − p_j), where δ_ij is the Kronecker delta (1 if i=j else 0). Diagonal entries are p_i(1−p_i); off-diagonal entries are −p_i p_j.
key_points.source: Standard result; Kurbiel, 'Derivative of the Softmax Function and the Categorical Cross-Entropy Loss'

key_points.point: The key headline result: composing softmax with cross-entropy gives dL/dz_j = p_j − y_j. All quotient-rule and 1/p_i terms cancel because the true-class term contributes the −y_j and the p_j·Σy_i term collapses since the one-hot vector sums to 1.
key_points.source: GeeksforGeeks, 'Derivative of the Softmax Function and the Categorical Cross-Entropy Loss'

key_points.point: U-Net (Ronneberger, Fischer, Brox, MICCAI 2015) defines its training objective as a pixel-wise soft-max over the final feature map combined with a cross-entropy loss — the 'energy function' E = Σ_x w(x) log(p_{ℓ(x)}(x)) — the direct ancestor of BraTS segmentation losses.
key_points.source: Ronneberger et al., U-Net: Convolutional Networks for Biomedical Image Segmentation (2015), arXiv:1505.04597

key_points.point: Because of the clean p − y gradient, frameworks fuse softmax and cross-entropy into one numerically stable operation that takes raw logits (PyTorch nn.CrossEntropyLoss, TF softmax_cross_entropy_with_logits) — you should NOT apply softmax yourself before these functions.

In segmentation (BraTS), this per-voxel cross-entropy is averaged (or class-weighted) over all voxels and is frequently combined with a Dice loss to counter severe class imbalance between tiny tumor regions and large background.
key_points.source: Isensee et al., nnU-Net, Nature Methods 2021

equations.name: Softmax function
equations.variables_explained: z = (z_1,...,z_K) is the vector of K raw logits (real numbers) output by the last layer for one voxel. z_i is the logit for class i. e is Euler's number (~2.718). p_i is the predicted probability of class i; the denominator S = Σ_k e^{z_k} normalizes so that all p_i are positive and sum to 1. K is the number of classes.

equations.name: Categorical cross-entropy loss (one example)
equations.variables_explained: y = (y_1,...,y_K) is the one-hot ground-truth label: y_c = 1 for the true class c and y_i = 0 otherwise. p_i is the softmax probability for class i. log is the natural logarithm. Because only the true-class term survives, L = -log(p_c). L ≥ 0, and L → 0 as p_c → 1.

equations.name: Softmax Jacobian
equations.variables_explained: This is the derivative of output probability p_i with respect to input logit z_j. δ_ij is the Kronecker delta: δ_ij = 1 when i = j, else 0. So the diagonal (i=j) is p_i(1 − p_i) and off-diagonal (i≠j) is −p_i p_j. It is a K×K matrix and is symmetric.

equations.name: Cross-entropy derivative w.r.t. probability
equations.variables_explained: How the loss changes as the predicted probability p_i changes. Since L = -Σ_i y_i log(p_i) and d/dp_i[log p_i] = 1/p_i, each term differentiates to −y_i/p_i. Only the true class (y_i=1) contributes a nonzero term.

equations.name: Headline gradient (softmax + cross-entropy)
equations.variables_explained: The gradient of the combined loss with respect to the raw logit z_j is simply the predicted probability minus the target. In vector form ∇_z L = p − y. Every component lies in (−1, 1). This is the error signal backpropagated into the network.

equations.name: U-Net energy (pixel-wise softmax + cross-entropy)
equations.variables_explained: From Ronneberger et al. (2015). x indexes pixels/voxels over the image domain Ω. ℓ(x) is the true label at x. p_{ℓ(x)}(x) is the softmax probability the network gives the correct class at x. w(x) is a per-pixel weight map (upweighting boundaries / rare classes). Minimizing cross-entropy = maximizing this weighted log-likelihood E.

derivations.title: Step 1 — Derivative of softmax: the diagonal case (i = j)
steps: p_i = \dfrac{e^{z_i}}{S}, \quad S = \sum_{k=1}^{K} e^{z_k}. — We write softmax as a quotient of e^{z_i} over the sum S of all exponentiated logits. We differentiate this with respect to one logit z_j.

\dfrac{\partial S}{\partial z_j} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial z_j}\sum_{k} e^{z_k} = e^{z_j}. — The sum S depends on z_j through exactly one term, e^{z_j}; every other term is constant w.r.t. z_j, so the derivative of the whole sum is just e^{z_j}.

\dfrac{\partial p_i}{\partial z_i} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial z_i}\left(\dfrac{e^{z_i}}{S}\right) = \dfrac{(\partial_{z_i} e^{z_i})\,S - e^{z_i}\,(\partial_{z_i} S)}{S^2}. — Apply the quotient rule (f/g)' = (f'g − fg')/g² with f = e^{z_i}, g = S. Here i = j so both numerator and denominator depend on z_i.
= \dfrac{e^{z_i} S - e^{z_i} e^{z_i}}{S^2}. — Substitute ∂_{z_i} e^{z_i} = e^{z_i} and ∂_{z_i} S = e^{z_i} from the previous step.

= \dfrac{e^{z_i}}{S} - \dfrac{e^{z_i}}{S}\cdot\dfrac{e^{z_i}}{S} = p_i - p_i^2 = p_i(1 - p_i). — Split the fraction into two pieces and recognize e^{z_i}/S = p_i in each. Factor out p_i to get the clean diagonal result.

derivations.title: Step 2 — Derivative of softmax: the off-diagonal case (i ≠ j)
steps: \dfrac{\partial p_i}{\partial z_j} = \dfrac{(\partial_{z_j} e^{z_i})\,S - e^{z_i}\,(\partial_{z_j} S)}{S^2}. — Same quotient rule, but now we differentiate p_i w.r.t. a DIFFERENT logit z_j (i ≠ j).
\partial_{z_j} e^{z_i} = 0 \quad (i \neq j). — The numerator e^{z_i} does not contain z_j, so its derivative is zero. Only the denominator carries the dependence.

= \dfrac{0\cdot S - e^{z_i} e^{z_j}}{S^2} = -\dfrac{e^{z_i}}{S}\cdot\dfrac{e^{z_j}}{S} = -p_i p_j. — Substitute ∂_{z_j}S = e^{z_j}, drop the zero term, and split into two softmax factors. The off-diagonal derivative is −p_i p_j.

\dfrac{\partial p_i}{\partial z_j} = p_i(\delta_{ij} - p_j). — Unify both cases: when i=j the bracket is (1 − p_j) giving p_i(1−p_i); when i≠j the bracket is (0 − p_j) giving −p_i p_j. The Kronecker delta δ_ij encodes 'i equals j'.

derivations.title: Step 3 — Derivative of cross-entropy w.r.t. the probabilities
steps: L = -\sum_{i=1}^{K} y_i \log(p_i). — The categorical cross-entropy loss. y_i is the one-hot target, p_i the predicted probability.

\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial p_i} = -y_i\cdot\dfrac{\partial}{\partial p_i}\log(p_i) = -\dfrac{y_i}{p_i}. — Differentiate term by term. The only term depending on p_i is −y_i log(p_i); using d[log p_i]/dp_i = 1/p_i gives −y_i/p_i. (We treat the p_i as independent here; their coupling is handled by the softmax Jacobian in Step 4.)

derivations.title: Step 4 — Chain rule: compose to get dL/dz_j and watch it collapse to p_j − y_j
steps: \dfrac{\partial L}{\partial z_j} = \sum_{i=1}^{K} \dfrac{\partial L}{\partial p_i}\,\dfrac{\partial p_i}{\partial z_j}. — The multivariate chain rule: z_j influences the loss through EVERY probability p_i (softmax couples all outputs), so we sum the contribution over all i.
= \sum_{i=1}^{K} \left(-\dfrac{y_i}{p_i}\right)\big(p_i(\delta_{ij} - p_j)\big). — Substitute the cross-entropy derivative from Step 3 and the softmax Jacobian from Steps 1–2.
= \sum_{i=1}^{K} -y_i(\delta_{ij} - p_j). — The p_i in the numerator of the Jacobian cancels the 1/p_i from the loss derivative. This cancellation is the whole reason the final result is so clean.
= -\sum_{i=1}^{K} y_i\,\delta_{ij} + \sum_{i=1}^{K} y_i\,p_j. — Distribute the −y_i across the bracket and split into two sums.
= -y_j + p_j\sum_{i=1}^{K} y_i. — First sum: Σ_i y_i δ_ij picks out only the i=j term, leaving y_j. Second sum: p_j does not depend on the summation index i, so factor it out of Σ_i y_i.

= -y_j + p_j\cdot 1 = p_j - y_j. — Use the defining property of a one-hot (or any valid probability) label: Σ_i y_i = 1. The second term becomes simply p_j. Result: dL/dz_j = p_j − y_j. In vector form ∇_z L = p − y. QED.

derivations.title: Step 5 — Numeric worked example (K = 3), full substitution
steps: z = (2.0,\ 1.0,\ 0.1),\quad y = (1,\ 0,\ 0)\ \text{(true class} = 0). — Three logits and a one-hot label saying class 0 is correct.
e^{2.0}=7.389,\ e^{1.0}=2.718,\ e^{0.1}=1.105,\quad S = 7.389+2.718+1.105 = 11.212. — Exponentiate each logit and sum to get the softmax denominator S.
p = \left(\tfrac{7.389}{11.212},\ \tfrac{2.718}{11.212},\ \tfrac{1.105}{11.212}\right) = (0.659,\ 0.242,\ 0.099). — Divide each exponentiated logit by S. The three probabilities sum to 1.000.
L = -\log(p_0) = -\log(0.659) = 0.417. — Cross-entropy with a one-hot label is just the negative log of the true-class probability (class 0).

\nabla_z L = p - y = (0.659-1,\ 0.242-0,\ 0.099-0) = (-0.341,\ 0.242,\ 0.099). — Apply the headline formula. The true class gets a negative gradient (push its logit UP), the wrong classes get positive gradients (push their logits DOWN). Components sum to 0, as they must since Σp=Σy=1.

intuitions: The gradient p − y is a 'prediction error' in probability space. If the model already outputs the correct answer with certainty (p = y), the gradient is zero and no update happens. The more confidently wrong the model is, the larger the push — but never larger than 1 per class, which keeps training stable.

Softmax is a 'soft argmax': it picks the largest logit as the most probable class but leaves smooth, differentiable probability mass on the others so gradients can flow. Cross-entropy then rewards putting probability mass on the true class and heavily punishes assigning near-zero probability to it (because −log(p) → ∞ as p → 0).

The magic cancellation happens because cross-entropy's 1/p_i term is exactly the inverse of the p_i that the softmax Jacobian produces. Softmax and cross-entropy are 'conjugate' — they were practically made for each other, which is why frameworks fuse them into one op.

The gradient components always sum to zero (Σ_j (p_j − y_j) = 1 − 1 = 0). Softmax is shift-invariant (adding a constant to all logits changes nothing), so the loss cannot 'care' about the overall level of the logits — only their differences. The zero-sum gradient reflects exactly that redundant direction.
gotchas: Do NOT apply softmax yourself and then feed the probabilities into a cross-entropy / NLL function that also assumes logits. PyTorch's nn.CrossEntropyLoss expects RAW logits and applies log-softmax internally; passing already-softmaxed values double-applies softmax and silently degrades training. Use nn.NLLLoss only if you applied log_softmax yourself.

Naively computing log(softmax(z)) risks numerical overflow (e^{z} for large z) or log(0) = −∞ for tiny probabilities. The fix is the log-sum-exp trick: subtract max(z) before exponentiating (softmax is invariant to this shift) and combine log and softmax analytically as z_i − logΣ_k e^{z_k}. This is why the fused logits-based loss is numerically safer than doing the two steps separately.

The clean result dL/dz = p − y holds only when y is a valid distribution summing to 1 (one-hot, or a soft label from label smoothing / mixup). If y does not sum to 1, the second sum p_j·Σy_i no longer collapses to p_j and the formula changes.

In BraTS segmentation, plain per-voxel cross-entropy is dominated by the huge background class and can ignore tiny tumor regions. Practitioners add class weights w(x) (as in the U-Net energy function) or combine cross-entropy with Dice loss. The p − y gradient still applies to the cross-entropy component, but the overall gradient is the weighted sum.

'Categorical' cross-entropy (one-hot integer labels, softmax over K classes) and 'binary' cross-entropy (sigmoid, per-class independent) are different. For K=2, softmax+categorical CE reduces exactly to sigmoid+binary CE — but for K>2 multi-LABEL problems (a voxel can belong to several overlapping regions, as in BraTS whole-tumor / tumor-core / enhancing hierarchies) you want per-class sigmoid + binary CE, not softmax.

example_questions.question: For logits z = (1, 3, 0) with true class index 1, compute the softmax probabilities, the cross-entropy loss, and the gradient dL/dz. Verify the gradient sums to zero.
example_questions.answer: Exponentiate: e^1 = 2.718, e^3 = 20.086, e^0 = 1.000. Sum S = 23.804. Softmax p = (2.718/23.804, 20.086/23.804, 1.000/23.804) = (0.1142, 0.8438, 0.0420); these sum to 1.000. One-hot label y = (0, 1, 0), so loss L = −log(p_1) = −log(0.8438) = 0.1699. Gradient (headline formula p − y): dL/dz = (0.1142 − 0, 0.8438 − 1, 0.0420 − 0) = (0.1142, −0.1562, 0.0420). Check: 0.1142 − 0.1562 + 0.0420 = 0.0000. The true class (index 1) has a negative gradient, so gradient descent increases its logit; the two wrong classes get pushed down. Sum is zero as required.

example_questions.question: Show explicitly why the 1/p_i term in the cross-entropy derivative disappears, using the true-class term. Why is the cancellation what makes the result numerically safe?
example_questions.answer: The chain-rule term for a given output i is (∂L/∂p_i)(∂p_i/∂z_j) = (−y_i/p_i)·(p_i(δ_ij − p_j)). The p_i in the numerator of the softmax Jacobian multiplies the 1/p_i from the loss derivative to give (−y_i)(δ_ij − p_j) — the p_i is gone. This matters because 1/p_i blows up when p_i is tiny (a class the model thinks is very unlikely), which would create enormous, unstable gradients. After cancellation the gradient is bounded: each component p_j − y_j lies strictly in (−1, 1). So the mathematical cancellation is also the reason fused softmax-cross-entropy avoids overflow/underflow that separate softmax then log then divide would suffer.

example_questions.question: A binary example: logits z = (z_0, z_1), true class 1. Show that softmax + categorical cross-entropy reduces to the sigmoid + binary cross-entropy form.
example_questions.answer: Softmax for class 1: p_1 = e^{z_1}/(e^{z_0}+e^{z_1}). Divide numerator and denominator by e^{z_1}: p_1 = 1/(1 + e^{z_0−z_1}) = 1/(1 + e^{−(z_1−z_0)}) = σ(z_1 − z_0), the logistic sigmoid of the logit DIFFERENCE Δ = z_1 − z_0. So a 2-class softmax depends only on one effective logit Δ, exactly like a single-output sigmoid. Cross-entropy with true class 1 is L = −log(p_1) = −log(σ(Δ)), which is precisely the binary cross-entropy for a positive example. The gradient dL/dΔ = σ(Δ) − 1 = p_1 − y_1, matching the general p − y result. This is why binary classifiers are usually built with one sigmoid output rather than a 2-way softmax — they are mathematically identical but the sigmoid uses half the parameters in the final layer.

Annotate the backward arrow underneath with 'gradient = p − y'.

A heatmap of the 3×3 softmax Jacobian for a concrete p = (0.66, 0.24, 0.10): diagonal cells labeled p_i(1−p_i) in one color, off-diagonal cells −p_i p_j in another, with the actual numbers filled in — this visually anchors the δ_ij(1) vs −p_j structure and shows the matrix is symmetric.

confidence_notes: All mathematics (softmax Jacobian, cross-entropy derivative, the p − y collapse, and both numeric examples) was derived and arithmetic-checked by hand and is standard, unambiguous, and independently corroborated by the cited references (GeeksforGeeks, Kurbiel/TDS). Numeric values are rounded to 3–4 significant figures; tiny rounding residuals (e.g., probability sums showing 1.000±0.001) are expected. The U-Net energy-function equation E = Σ_x w(x) log(p_{ℓ(x)}(x)) and the 'pixel-wise softmax + cross-entropy' framing are taken from the Ronneberger et al. 2015 paper (arXiv:1505.04597); I cited the arXiv abstract page rather than re-fetching the full PDF text in this session, but this is a very widely reproduced equation. The nnU-Net Dice+CE combination and PyTorch CrossEntropyLoss logits-input behavior are well documented at the cited URLs. No clinical claims are made here — this is pure ML mathematics — so no medical sourcing was required.
